title: New executable ran from /tmp
summary: A binary at /tmp/build-9f2/configure ran for the first time. Parent chain: bash -> make -> configure.

explain.what: A program that had never run before executed from /tmp.
explain.why: Attackers stage payloads in world-writable directories because they survive no reboot and leave no package trail. Build systems do it too, which is why this is low.
explain.expected: Anything you build from source: configure scripts, cargo/go build output, unpacked tarballs.
next: Nothing, if you started this build. Otherwise check what wrote /tmp/build-9f2.

title: npm install reached a host that is not a package registry
summary: node (pid 33871), under npm, connected to 185.199.108.153:443 (cdn.jsdelivr.net). Parent chain: npm -> node.

explain.what: A postinstall script inside an npm install opened a connection to a host that is not a package registry.
explain.why: Registry installs only need registry hosts. A postinstall that phones somewhere else is how dependency-confusion and telemetry-exfil packages behave.
evidence: host not in registry allowlist [registry.npmjs.org, pypi.org, crates.io, github.com, *.archlinux.org]
explain.expected: Packages that fetch prebuilt binaries at install time (esbuild, sharp, playwright) legitimately hit CDNs.
next: Read node_modules/telemetry-lite/postinstall.js before you run the project.
If the package is not one you chose, check the lockfile diff for who pulled it in.

title: Private SSH key read by an unexpected program
summary: node (pid 41233) read /home/dan/.ssh/id_rsa. Parent chain: npm -> node -> sh -> node.

explain.what: node read your private SSH key.
explain.why: Private keys are the first thing npm and PyPI stealers read; only ssh, git and a few tools ever need them.
evidence: ancestry: npm -> node -> sh -> node (package install in /home/dan/proj)
not in allowlist: exe not in [ssh, ssh-agent, ssh-keygen, git, scp, sftp, rsync]
explain.expected: Backup tools, IDE git integrations, and custom scripts that call ssh libraries.
next: If you did not expect this: kill the process, then rotate the key (ssh-keygen -t ed25519, replace the public key on GitHub and servers).
Check what was installed: look at the npm/pip lockfile diff and the package's postinstall script.

title: AI CLI ran with permission checks disabled and no terminal
summary: claude (pid 41390) ran with --dangerously-skip-permissions under an npm postinstall, with no interactive shell in its ancestry.

explain.what: An AI coding agent was started with its permission prompts turned off, by a package install rather than by you.
explain.why: --dangerously-skip-permissions lets the agent run any command without asking. Started from a postinstall with no terminal attached, nobody is there to approve anything.
evidence: ancestry: npm -> node -> claude (no interactive shell, no controlling tty)
rule: sentinel-x-ai-cli-headless (userland, not a Tetragon policy)
explain.expected: CI jobs and your own scripted agent runs. Not an npm postinstall.
next: Kill it, then read the postinstall script that started it.
Sign out of the Claude CLI and back in; treat any credential under ~/.claude as exposed.

title: Shell startup file modified
summary: sh (pid 41402) appended to /home/dan/.bashrc. Parent chain: npm -> node -> sh.

explain.what: Something appended a command to your ~/.bashrc.
explain.why: A line in a shell rc file runs on every new terminal. It is the cheapest persistence there is, and the appended text here fetches and pipes a remote script to a shell.
evidence: appended text matches pattern: curl piped to shell
explain.expected: Installers you ran on purpose (mise, nvm, rustup) append to shell rc files during setup.
next: Open ~/.bashrc and delete the appended line.
Check ~/.zshrc, ~/.profile and ~/.config/autostart for the same pattern.

title: Reverse shell: a shell with its stdio on a socket
summary: sh (pid 41455) started with stdin/stdout bound to 45.61.0.9:4444. Parent chain: npm -> node -> sh.

explain.what: An interactive shell started with its input and output attached to a network socket. That is a remote operator typing on your machine.
explain.why: No legitimate program gives a shell a socket for stdin. This pattern has no benign version.
explain.expected: Nothing. There is no expected version of this.
next: Kill it now, then disconnect from the network before anything else.
Assume every credential this user account can reach is compromised: SSH keys, tokens, browser sessions.
Preserve /var/log/sentinel/tetragon.log before you reboot.

title: A newly executed binary matches a known-malware hash
summary: /dev/shm/.x (pid 41470) executed; its sha256 is in the MalwareBazaar feed.

explain.what: A binary staged in /dev/shm ran, and its hash is on a public malware feed.
explain.why: A hash match against MalwareBazaar is not heuristic. This exact file has been seen and classified as malware elsewhere.
next: Kill and quarantine it, then treat the machine as compromised.
Rotate every credential reachable from this account before using them again.

title: Cloud credentials file read by an unexpected program
summary: python3 (pid 41902) read /home/dan/.aws/credentials. Parent chain: pip -> python3.

explain.what: A python process started by pip read your AWS credentials file.
explain.why: pip's dependency chain has no business reading long-lived cloud keys. This is the standard second step after a malicious sdist gains execution.
evidence: process: /usr/bin/python3 pid 41902, inline -c reading the credentials file
not in allowlist: exe not in [aws, terraform, aws-vault, boto-using apps you approved]
explain.expected: The aws CLI, terraform, and SDK-based apps you run yourself.
next: Deactivate then delete the access key in IAM and create a new one.
Review CloudTrail for use of the old key from an address you do not recognize.

title: A setuid binary was created in a user-writable directory
summary: chmod (pid 42010) set the setuid bit on /tmp/.helper, owner root.

explain.what: The setuid bit was set on a file in /tmp, so anyone running it gets its owner's privileges.
explain.why: A root-owned setuid binary in a world-writable directory is a privilege-escalation backdoor. Packages never install one there.
evidence: path is under a world-writable directory
explain.expected: Nothing outside of a package manager writing to /usr.
next: Quarantine /tmp/.helper, then find out what ran sudo in that shell.
Check /etc/sudoers.d and your sudo timestamp directory for other changes.

title: An out-of-tree kernel module was loaded

explain.what: A kernel module was loaded from /tmp, outside the module tree the kernel ships.
explain.why: A loaded module runs in ring 0 and can hide processes, files and network connections from everything above it, including this monitor.
explain.expected: Nothing. DKMS modules load from /usr/lib/modules, not /tmp.
next: Do not trust anything this machine reports from here on, including Sentinel.
Power it off and reinstall. Rotate every credential from another machine.

title: One process read 63 files across your dotdirs in 10 seconds
summary: trufflehog-like read pattern: node (pid 42501) opened 63 distinct files under /home/dan/.config, /home/dan/.aws and /home/dan/.gnupg.

explain.what: A single process walked your dotdirectories and opened 63 files in ten seconds.
explain.why: That is a secret-scanning sweep, not a program reading its own config. The threshold is 40 distinct files in 10 seconds.
explain.expected: Backup tools and search indexers (ripgrep on your home, restic, a dotfile manager).
next: Kill it, then rotate the GitHub, npm and GPG credentials it could reach.
Remove node_modules and reinstall from a lockfile you trust.

title: Connection to a host on the ThreatFox feed
summary: curl (pid 42760) connected to 91.219.236.18:8080 (updates-cdn.top), listed by ThreatFox.

explain.what: curl fetched from a domain that is on a current threat-intelligence feed.
explain.why: updates-cdn.top is listed by ThreatFox as command-and-control infrastructure. Feed hits are not proof, but they are not noise either.
explain.expected: Nothing you would recognize. Feeds do carry false positives on shared hosting.
next: Find the script in your shell history that ran this curl, and read what it does with the response.

title: New executable ran from your home directory
summary: A binary at /home/dan/.local/bin/lazygit ran for the first time.

explain.what: A program under /home/dan/.local/bin executed for the first time.
explain.why: New executables in $HOME are how user-level malware persists, and also how every tool you install by hand arrives. Hence low.
explain.expected: Anything you installed with go install, cargo install, pipx, or a release tarball.
next: Nothing, if you installed it.
